misreading.wrong: What history cannot document cannot be real; the Christ of faith is a pious overlay added to the merely human Jesus.
misreading.right: The documentary method is the limit: it checks papers, not persons; the Christ belongs to the event, not to later belief.
misreading.quote: the full truth of history eludes documentary verification just as much as the truth of being escapes the experimental approach

argument.tension: The Creed binds the meaning of all being to one executed man, yet critical history can check only documents, not depths.
argument.move: He parallels physics: methodical precision renounces being, so historical method likewise reveals the surface while concealing history's full truth.
argument.payoff: Not faith but positivism shrinks the past; the Christ can be a truth of history even when undocumentable.

misreading.wrong: Historical criticism dissolved the plain Jesus, so faith should rest on the preached kerygma alone; the historical Jesus is irrelevant.
misreading.right: Both flights fail: bare history creates no present, bare kerygma an empty event; Jesus subsists only as Christ, Christ only as Jesus.
misreading.quote: But is an empty event any easier to swallow than one filled with content?

argument.tension: Modern theology flees from Christ to a recoverable Jesus, then from Jesus to a bare kerygma, and now back again.
argument.move: The zig-zag is wasted motion yet proves the two cannot subsist apart; faith confesses their unity rather than reconstructing either.
argument.payoff: Reconstruction and reduction are both barred; one may simply hear what the living faith of centuries has always stated.

rubric: faith is living presence, not reconstruction

misreading.wrong: Once "Christ" hardened into a title and the Creed fixed it in dogma, the living person of Jesus disappeared behind formulas.
misreading.right: The fused name-title safeguards the person: faith accepts this person who is his word, not a detachable system of teaching.
misreading.quote: Such faith is not the acceptance of a system but the acceptance of this person who is his word

argument.tension: In "Christ Jesus" a title has fused with a name, just as "Kaiser" fused with "Wilhelm"—accident or insight?
argument.move: The fusion is no lapse of memory but faith's core: with Jesus, person and office, existence and mission, are one.
argument.payoff: Faith becomes personal: no private "I" lurks behind his work, so doctrine can never replace the person it names.

misreading.wrong: Jesus' death is a moving example of fidelity unto death; the Cross shows how a good man faces suffering.
misreading.right: The Cross is faith's birthplace: Pilate's execution notice became the first creed—the crucified criminal is the Christ, the King.
misreading.quote: This execution notice, the death sentence of history, became with paradoxical unity the “profession of faith”

argument.tension: Jesus never called himself Messiah; yet faith in Jesus as Christ began somewhere—with his preaching or elsewhere?
argument.move: Pilate's death sentence naming the executed "King of the Jews" turns, paradoxically, into the first profession of faith.
argument.payoff: Seen from the Cross, person, word, and work are one; only then are his words reread and John's logos drawn.

misreading.wrong: Firm dogmatic faith in Christ's divinity breeds exclusivism and lovelessness; love grows only where doctrine is loosened.
misreading.right: The hyphen joining Jesus to Christ joins faith to love: believing means discovering Christ in the least of men and serving them.
misreading.quote: faith that is not love is not a really Christian faith; it only seems to be such

argument.tension: Harnack's charge: does confessing Christ the Son divide people and bury the simple message of love under dogma?
argument.move: His "I" is pure relation—derived from the Father, lived for men—so logos and love coincide; faith must become love.
argument.payoff: Mt 25 follows from Christology's heart: service is no escape from dogma but the hyphen's logical consequence.

misreading.wrong: If Jesus is truly God, his humanity is a shell; high Christology necessarily makes the merely human second-rate.
misreading.right: Dogma answers both questions Yes: an existence that is love is God's; the radical servant is the truest man—theology and anthropology coincide.
misreading.quote: in the radicality of his service Jesus is the most human of men, the true man

argument.tension: Jesus' "I" is pure openness, all word, all son: is such an existence God's, or merely humanity's perfection?
argument.move: From the Creed itself the councils draw a triple Yes, holding radical Christship, Sonship, Godship, and true humanity together.
argument.payoff: Dogma is not Greek overkill but loyalty to the original confession—the safeguard of the whole, logos-like rather than myth.

misreading.wrong: The standard account—failed prophet, resurrection rumor, Hellenistic myth, Chalcedon—is sober historical scholarship; faith simply refuses the evidence.
misreading.right: The stock story is itself a conglomeration of hypotheses; as history it is absurd—harder to believe than God's becoming man.
misreading.quote: To anyone accustomed to think historically, the whole theory is absurd, even if today hordes of people believe it

argument.tension: A vulgarized modern story claims historical pedigree: prophetic teacher, failed death, mythic overlay, then dogma ratified at Chalcedon.
argument.move: He turns historical scrutiny on the reconstruction itself and finds hypothesis stacked on hypothesis—less credible than the dogma it dissolves.
argument.payoff: Even apart from faith, acquaintance with history makes the Incarnation the more reasonable belief; the stock idea self-destructs.

misreading.wrong: Kenosis means God empties out his power; self-emptying abolishes divine lordship and leaves only divine weakness.
misreading.right: Self-emptying is pure relatedness: not clinging to himself, he coincides with the absolute; the servant is Lord in, not despite, surrender.
misreading.quote: he who does not cling to himself but is pure relatedness coincides in this with the absolute

argument.tension: Phil 2 joins utter abasement with cosmic lordship; the slaughtered Lamb receives the universe's proskynesis—how can both hold?
argument.move: The demythologized title "Son of God" reaches its goal at the Cross: being that is pure service coincides with God.
argument.payoff: Kenosis is not power's cancellation but its true form; dogma names this identity of service and being.

misreading.wrong: Christians must choose: Greek metaphysics of Incarnation or the Reformers' theology of the Cross; being and event contradict each other.
misreading.right: No flattening synthesis: the polarities mutually correct, yet each fully thought passes into the other—Christ's being is act, his act being.
misreading.quote: this “doing” is not just “doing” but “being”; it reaches down into the depths of being and coincides with it

argument.tension: Incarnation theology speaks of being, God-man unity; Cross theology speaks of event, God's act conquering death—irreconcilable centres?
argument.move: He keeps the polarities, then shows Christ's being is actualitas, exodus from self, so each theology must pass into the other.
argument.payoff: Two centres of one mystery correct each other and, complementing, point toward the whole; neither may absorb the other.

misreading.wrong: Redemption is a transaction: God demanded infinite payment and collected it from his tortured Son—divine child abuse dressed as justice.
misreading.right: Anselm grasps the biblical "for" and election as call to live for others, yet his rigid legal system distorts perspectives and darkens God.
misreading.quote: the perfectly logical divine-cum-human legal system erected by Anselm distorts the perspectives

argument.tension: Christology (who Jesus is) and soteriology (what he does) split into separate treatises—does either remain intelligible alone?
argument.move: Reuniting person and work, he reads redemption as being human, not having it—the last Adam taking humanity into God's future.
argument.payoff: The legal picture yields to the personal: not payment but humanity's healing and union with God in the "last man".

misreading.wrong: Christ the "last man" heralds cheerful progress: humanity is steadily evolving upward, and Christ is its inspiring symbol.
misreading.right: No progress-romanticism: the man for others is sacrificed man; humanity's future hangs on the Cross, whose pierced openness gathers all.
misreading.quote: how little it really has to do with the cheerful romanticism of progress

argument.tension: Man comes to himself only by moving beyond himself; can one man's existence really gather all humanity into its future?
argument.move: Christ the "last Adam" is the exemplary man whose open, pierced existence draws all into one body—true humanity's form.
argument.payoff: Humanity's fulfilment is "being for": the Cross, not progress, is man's future, and the last man appears in the last men.
